items.title: BYDFi’s Up to 8,100 USDT Welcome Rewards: A Security-First Guide for New Users
items.summary: BYDFi’s September 2026 platform upgrade, BYDFi Revamp, brings campaigns, tasks, and reward claims together in a single Rewards Hub, where new users can explore crypto welcome rewards for new users of up to 8,100 USDT. From a security perspective, a welcome offer is also an onboarding window in which an account goes from empty to funded while its owner is still learning the interface, the official domains, and what a legitimate notification looks like. That window is exactly what credential phishers, SIM swappers, and wallet-drainer operators plan their campaigns around. This guide treats the BYDFi offer as a threat model as well as a promotion: what attackers target at each step, which controls BYDFi exposes to block them, and how to configure those controls before any USDT is at risk. How to get started securely Register through the official page. Type the address yourself or use a bookmark; never follow a link from a message or search ad. Sign up using an email address, phone number, or Google, Apple, or Telegram account. A dedicated email address used only for crypto limits the blast radius if another account is ever breached. Harden the account before you fund it. Set up passkey sign-in with Face ID or Touch ID. Passkeys are bound to the real BYDFi domain, so a cloned login page cannot use them; Cyber Security News explains how this biometric authentication model works. Then enable Google Authenticator, create an anti-phishing code, and turn on the withdrawal whitelist. With the whitelist restriction on, newly added addresses must wait 24 hours before they can receive funds, which gives you a window to catch and reverse an unauthorized change. Complete identity verification. BYDFi offers Primary KYC and Advanced KYC. Completing verification early unlocks tasks that require it and makes account recovery far easier if you are ever locked out. Submit documents only inside the BYDFi app or website, never to a “verification agent” who messages you. Visit the Rewards Hub. Review the available tasks, their requirements, and deadlines. Your progress and claim buttons are also shown there. If a reward is real, it is visible here after you log in; anything that exists only in an email or chat should be treated as suspect. Choose how you want to explore BYDFi. Crypto deposits are free. If you buy crypto with a card, the minimum purchase is the equivalent of 50 USD. Only deposit and trade amounts that fit your own plans and risk tolerance. Try the available tools. If you are new to futures, practise first in Demo Trading, which requires a BYDFi login. You can also explore spot trading, Convert, Copy Trading (from 30 USDT), and trading bots such as Futures Grid (from 10 USDT). Explore the 8,100 USDT Welcome Reward Package The BYDFi welcome reward package gives new users several ways to get more from their first steps on the platform. If you are weighing up crypto welcome rewards for new users , the structure here is simple: eligible tasks are organized around four milestones: Sign Up, KYC, Deposit, and Trade. Depending on the campaign and your eligibility, rewards include a BTCUSDT Position Airdrop, USDT Futures Bonus, and USDT Vouchers. Milestone What it involves Security note Sign Up Create the account through the official page Enable passkey and 2FA before anything else KYC Primary or Advanced identity verification Upload documents only inside the BYDFi app or site Deposit Fund the account by crypto or card Use the withdrawal whitelist; verify deposit addresses in-app Trade Spot, futures, Copy Trading, or bots Start in Demo Trading; keep leverage conservative These rewards can help you explore different BYDFi features. Futures Bonuses can be used for USDT-M futures trading. Vouchers may provide benefits such as token rewards, fee offsets, or an APR boost for a specified Earn product. Check each reward’s terms in the Rewards Hub to see how it can be used. Every claim happens inside your logged-in account; BYDFi never asks you to “unlock” a reward by sending funds or sharing a code. Explore more campaigns in the Event Center The Event Center is separate from the Rewards Hub and features limited-time promotions across futures, spot, referrals, fiat, and selected regions. For example, BYDFi’s past 0-Fee Fest offered 0% maker and taker fees on selected futures pairs for a limited time. Event requirements and payout schedules vary. Some events are first come, first served, while others may take up to 7 business days after the event ends to pay out. Check each event’s terms for its eligibility requirements and reward timeline. From a security standpoint, the payout delay matters: scammers often exploit the waiting period by impersonating support and offering to “speed up” a payout for a fee or a login code. Legitimate payouts arrive in your account without any action on your part. What to know about Futures Bonuses A Futures Bonus is trial credit for USDT-M futures. You can withdraw profits earned using the bonus, while the bonus amount itself cannot be withdrawn. Futures use leverage, which can magnify both gains and losses, and positions can be liquidated. BYDFi lists limited-time leverage of up to 500x for BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT, with lower caps on other contracts, for example up to 300x on DOGEUSDT and up to 100x on SOLUSDT. Available leverage decreases as position size increases. Review the contract details carefully before trading. Check eligibility and current terms BYDFi serves users in more than 190 countries and regions, but product and promotion availability varies by location. Most rewards require identity verification, and each task may have its own eligibility rules and deadline. If you are unsure what applies in your country, contact BYDFi’s 24/7 support team at cs@bydfi.com. The Help Center also lists common reasons users may be unable to join events or claim rewards. The advertised 8,100 USDT is the maximum available across eligible tasks, rather than an amount automatically credited at registration. The rewards you can access depend on your account’s eligibility and completion of the applicable tasks within their deadlines. Check the live Rewards Hub for the offers currently available to you, since third-party blogs and coupon pages may display outdated figures. Inflated or “guaranteed” bonus claims on third-party sites are also a common lure for phishing pages, so treat any number that does not match the Rewards Hub as a red flag rather than a better deal. Protect your account Popular offers can attract impersonators. Fake websites and social accounts may copy exchange branding and ask for passwords or verification codes. Use BYDFi Verify at bydfi.com/official-verify to check whether an email address, phone number, website, Telegram handle, or X account belongs to BYDFi. Genuine BYDFi emails also include the anti-phishing code you set. BYDFi support will not ask for your password or a one-time code. Operational habits that close the remaining gaps Open BYDFi from a bookmark you created yourself, never from search results, ads, or messages. Before confirming any deposit or withdrawal, compare the first and last six characters of the address shown in-app against the destination. Clipboard-swapping malware relies on you not checking. Never type a seed phrase, private key, or one-time code into anything that is not the official app or site, including a “verification bot.” If you suspect compromise From a clean device, change your password and re-enroll 2FA, revoking the old authenticator. Review and terminate all active sessions and devices. Delete every API key and re-create only what you need. Check the withdrawal whitelist for addresses you did not add, and remove them. Contact cs@bydfi.com from the email address on the account, and report any impersonating site or handle through BYDFi Verify. Run a malware scan and rotate the password on the email account tied to BYDFi, since that mailbox is the recovery path. Awareness is the one layer attackers cannot patch around. Cyber Security News’ guide to social engineering tactics is a useful primer on the pressure techniques (urgency, authority, fear of missing out) that nearly every crypto scam relies on. Frequently asked questions Does every new user receive 8,100 USDT? 8,100 USDT is the maximum available across eligible tasks. The rewards you receive depend on your eligibility and the tasks you complete before their deadlines. Is KYC required? Most rewards require identity verification. Check the requirements shown for each task. Can I withdraw the Futures Bonus? The bonus itself cannot be withdrawn, but profits earned using it can be. How soon do rewards arrive? It depends on the reward. Some event payouts may take up to 7 business days after the event ends. Is the offer available in every country? Availability varies by region. Contact BYDFi support if you are unsure about your eligibility. The bottom line BYDFi brings spot and perpetual futures, USDT-margined futures on US stocks, gold and crude oil, Copy Trading, and automated bots together under one account, and the Rewards Hub gives eligible new users a clear place to explore available tasks and track their progress. The security takeaway is simple: the controls that defeat the attacks in this guide (passkeys, TOTP, the anti-phishing code, the withdrawal whitelist, and BYDFi Verify) are all available on day one and take about ten minutes to configure. Switch them on before the first deposit, verify every channel before you trust it, and treat the Rewards Hub as the only authoritative source for what you have earned. A welcome reward is only worth what you can keep.
items.summary_html:
BYDFi’s September 2026 platform upgrade, BYDFi Revamp, brings campaigns, tasks, and reward claims together in a single Rewards Hub, where new users can explore crypto welcome rewards for new users of up to 8,100 USDT. From a security perspective, a welcome offer is also an onboarding window in which an account goes from empty to funded while its owner is still learning the interface, the official domains, and what a legitimate notification looks like. That window is exactly what credential phishers, SIM swappers, and wallet-drainer operators plan their campaigns around. This guide treats the BYDFi offer as a threat model as well as a promotion: what attackers target at each step, which controls BYDFi exposes to block them, and how to configure those controls before any USDT is at risk. 

How to get started securely
  1. Register through the official page. Type the address yourself or use a bookmark; never follow a link from a message or search ad. Sign up using an email address, phone number, or Google, Apple, or Telegram account. A dedicated email address used only for crypto limits the blast radius if another account is ever breached.
  2. Harden the account before you fund it. Set up passkey sign-in with Face ID or Touch ID. Passkeys are bound to the real BYDFi domain, so a cloned login page cannot use them; Cyber Security News explains how this biometric authentication model works. Then enable Google Authenticator, create an anti-phishing code, and turn on the withdrawal whitelist. With the whitelist restriction on, newly added addresses must wait 24 hours before they can receive funds, which gives you a window to catch and reverse an unauthorized change.
  3. Complete identity verification. BYDFi offers Primary KYC and Advanced KYC. Completing verification early unlocks tasks that require it and makes account recovery far easier if you are ever locked out. Submit documents only inside the BYDFi app or website, never to a “verification agent” who messages you.
  4. Visit the Rewards Hub. Review the available tasks, their requirements, and deadlines. Your progress and claim buttons are also shown there. If a reward is real, it is visible here after you log in; anything that exists only in an email or chat should be treated as suspect.
  5. Choose how you want to explore BYDFi. Crypto deposits are free. If you buy crypto with a card, the minimum purchase is the equivalent of 50 USD. Only deposit and trade amounts that fit your own plans and risk tolerance.
  6. Try the available tools. If you are new to futures, practise first in Demo Trading, which requires a BYDFi login. You can also explore spot trading, Convert, Copy Trading (from 30 USDT), and trading bots such as Futures Grid (from 10 USDT).
Explore the 8,100 USDT Welcome Reward Package

The BYDFi welcome reward package gives new users several ways to get more from their first steps on the platform.  If you are weighing up crypto welcome rewards for new users, the structure here is simple: eligible tasks are organized around four milestones: Sign Up, KYC, Deposit, and Trade. Depending on the campaign and your eligibility, rewards include a BTCUSDT Position Airdrop, USDT Futures Bonus, and USDT Vouchers.

MilestoneWhat it involvesSecurity noteSign UpCreate the account through the official pageEnable passkey and 2FA before anything elseKYCPrimary or Advanced identity verificationUpload documents only inside the BYDFi app or siteDepositFund the account by crypto or cardUse the withdrawal whitelist; verify deposit addresses in-appTradeSpot, futures, Copy Trading, or botsStart in Demo Trading; keep leverage conservative

These rewards can help you explore different BYDFi features. Futures Bonuses can be used for USDT-M futures trading. Vouchers may provide benefits such as token rewards, fee offsets, or an APR boost for a specified Earn product. Check each reward’s terms in the Rewards Hub to see how it can be used. Every claim happens inside your logged-in account; BYDFi never asks you to “unlock” a reward by sending funds or sharing a code.

Explore more campaigns in the Event Center

The Event Center is separate from the Rewards Hub and features limited-time promotions across futures, spot, referrals, fiat, and selected regions. For example, BYDFi’s past 0-Fee Fest offered 0% maker and taker fees on selected futures pairs for a limited time.

Event requirements and payout schedules vary. Some events are first come, first served, while others may take up to 7 business days after the event ends to pay out. Check each event’s terms for its eligibility requirements and reward timeline. From a security standpoint, the payout delay matters: scammers often exploit the waiting period by impersonating support and offering to “speed up” a payout for a fee or a login code. Legitimate payouts arrive in your account without any action on your part.

What to know about Futures Bonuses

A Futures Bonus is trial credit for USDT-M futures. You can withdraw profits earned using the bonus, while the bonus amount itself cannot be withdrawn.

Futures use leverage, which can magnify both gains and losses, and positions can be liquidated. BYDFi lists limited-time leverage of up to 500x for BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT, with lower caps on other contracts, for example up to 300x on DOGEUSDT and up to 100x on SOLUSDT. Available leverage decreases as position size increases. Review the contract details carefully before trading.

Check eligibility and current terms

BYDFi serves users in more than 190 countries and regions, but product and promotion availability varies by location. Most rewards require identity verification, and each task may have its own eligibility rules and deadline. If you are unsure what applies in your country, contact BYDFi’s 24/7 support team at cs@bydfi.com. The Help Center also lists common reasons users may be unable to join events or claim rewards.

The advertised 8,100 USDT is the maximum available across eligible tasks, rather than an amount automatically credited at registration. The rewards you can access depend on your account’s eligibility and completion of the applicable tasks within their deadlines. Check the live Rewards Hub for the offers currently available to you, since third-party blogs and coupon pages may display outdated figures. Inflated or “guaranteed” bonus claims on third-party sites are also a common lure for phishing pages, so treat any number that does not match the Rewards Hub as a red flag rather than a better deal.

Protect your account

Popular offers can attract impersonators. Fake websites and social accounts may copy exchange branding and ask for passwords or verification codes. Use BYDFi Verify at bydfi.com/official-verify to check whether an email address, phone number, website, Telegram handle, or X account belongs to BYDFi. Genuine BYDFi emails also include the anti-phishing code you set. BYDFi support will not ask for your password or a one-time code.

Operational habits that close the remaining gaps

  • Open BYDFi from a bookmark you created yourself, never from search results, ads, or messages.
  • Before confirming any deposit or withdrawal, compare the first and last six characters of the address shown in-app against the destination. Clipboard-swapping malware relies on you not checking.
  • Never type a seed phrase, private key, or one-time code into anything that is not the official app or site, including a “verification bot.”

If you suspect compromise

  1. From a clean device, change your password and re-enroll 2FA, revoking the old authenticator.
  2. Review and terminate all active sessions and devices.
  3. Delete every API key and re-create only what you need.
  4. Check the withdrawal whitelist for addresses you did not add, and remove them.
  5. Contact cs@bydfi.com from the email address on the account, and report any impersonating site or handle through BYDFi Verify.
  6. Run a malware scan and rotate the password on the email account tied to BYDFi, since that mailbox is the recovery path.

Awareness is the one layer attackers cannot patch around. Cyber Security News’ guide to social engineering tactics is a useful primer on the pressure techniques (urgency, authority, fear of missing out) that nearly every crypto scam relies on.

Frequently asked questions

Does every new user receive 8,100 USDT? 8,100 USDT is the maximum available across eligible tasks. The rewards you receive depend on your eligibility and the tasks you complete before their deadlines.

Is KYC required? Most rewards require identity verification. Check the requirements shown for each task.

Can I withdraw the Futures Bonus? The bonus itself cannot be withdrawn, but profits earned using it can be.

How soon do rewards arrive? It depends on the reward. Some event payouts may take up to 7 business days after the event ends.

Is the offer available in every country? Availability varies by region. Contact BYDFi support if you are unsure about your eligibility.

The bottom line

BYDFi brings spot and perpetual futures, USDT-margined futures on US stocks, gold and crude oil, Copy Trading, and automated bots together under one account, and the Rewards Hub gives eligible new users a clear place to explore available tasks and track their progress. The security takeaway is simple: the controls that defeat the attacks in this guide (passkeys, TOTP, the anti-phishing code, the withdrawal whitelist, and BYDFi Verify) are all available on day one and take about ten minutes to configure. Switch them on before the first deposit, verify every channel before you trust it, and treat the Rewards Hub as the only authoritative source for what you have earned. A welcome reward is only worth what you can keep.

items.title: OpenAI Launches New Security Sprint to Hunt Vulnerabilities and Strengthen Defenses
items.summary: OpenAI is preparing a new internal security sprint that will bring outside researchers together with its own teams to find vulnerabilities, test fixes, and strengthen its platforms using AI. Announced on November 2, the effort includes a partnership with Cathedral Systems and higher bug bounty rewards to encourage independent researchers to report serious security flaws. The security sprint announcement describes a broader push toward continuous defense, where finding weaknesses and checking repairs becomes ongoing work rather than a one-time assessment. Cathedral researchers will use OpenAI models alongside company staff to challenge existing protections and bring fresh approaches to testing its systems. Cathedral Partnership Expands Security Testing Gavin Kliger, CEO and co-founder of Cathedral Systems, said the collaboration would combine his team’s research with OpenAI’s models and security expertise to find weaknesses, test fixes, and improve continuous defense. The announcement outlines the planned collaboration but does not provide a start date, target list, or vulnerability findings from the upcoming sprint. The effort builds on an earlier sprint in which OpenAI assigned 25% of its product engineers to security work. Engineers used Codex to investigate reports, reproduce vulnerabilities in isolated environments, and prepare patches for review. This approach ties AI-assisted vulnerability discovery to practical checks before proposed changes reach production systems. OpenAI’s published Defense Factory architecture explains how that process works. Agents map systems, investigate possible flaws, confirm whether issues can be reproduced, identify responsible teams, and prepare tested fixes. Isolated environments provide the code, services, and settings needed to test a suspected vulnerability without running experiments directly against live systems. The company also describes lessons from early testing. Duplicate findings slowed review, severity ratings needed clearer instructions, and missing dependencies made some tests difficult to run. OpenAI says follow-up checks exposed another important gap: a merged patch did not always mean the fix had reached every deployed system. Human review and independent checks therefore remain part of the workflow. This builds on the capabilities covered in Cybersecurity News’ report on OpenAI Codex Security , which examined the agent’s role in discovering, validating, and fixing software vulnerabilities. The new sprint applies that model-assisted approach to OpenAI’s own defenses with added outside research support. Higher Bug Bounties Alongside the sprint, OpenAI has increased Security Bug Bounty rewards . Critical vulnerabilities in core products, including ChatGPT, Codex, and the API Platform, can now earn up to $30,000. Exceptional critical findings remain eligible for a $100,000 base award, with bonuses bringing potential payouts to about $172,000. Report quality, researcher loyalty, and priority campaigns affect the final amount. These changes extend the program previously covered in OpenAI’s $100,000 bug bounty expansion . Researchers should distinguish normal critical rewards from exceptional awards rather than treat the highest advertised payout as standard. OpenAI is also connecting this work to Daybreak for Frontline Defenders , its $1 billion commitment to subsidized access, training, support, and partnerships over six months. The initiative targets essential services and organizations with limited security resources. Its stated goal mirrors the internal sprint: help defenders turn confirmed weaknesses into tested fixes, while keeping people responsible for consequential decisions. items.title: Anthropic Enables EDR Monitoring in Claude Cowork to Detect Hidden AI Agent Activity
items.summary: Anthropic has introduced a beta integration that lets businesses run endpoint detection and response sensors inside Claude Cowork’s local virtual machine. The feature addresses a monitoring gap: security software installed on a computer cannot see the shell commands and code Cowork runs inside its isolated environment. Teams can now send that activity to their existing security console. The EDR integration supports Team and Enterprise plans on macOS and Windows. It also works with Claude Desktop connected to Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry. Anthropic’s setup guidance makes one limit clear: coverage applies only to the local VM, not Cowork sessions hosted on Anthropic’s servers. Anthropic Enables EDR Monitoring Cowork uses a virtual machine to separate code execution from the user’s computer. That boundary also prevents the host computer’s EDR sensor from inspecting activity inside the guest environment. Installing a sensor within the VM gives security teams visibility into work that otherwise sits beyond their existing endpoint monitoring. The change matters as AI tools gain more freedom to act. Cybersecurity News previously covered Claude’s background computer use , which lets the assistant interact with desktop applications. That capability is distinct from sandboxed code execution, but both raise questions about how organizations monitor automated actions. Earlier reporting on a Claude Cowork sandbox vulnerability also showed why activity inside these environments deserves attention. That research described a Windows attack chain leading to root access within the Linux sandbox. The new monitoring feature should not be confused with a fix for that reported flaw. Each time the Cowork VM starts, Claude Desktop copies the configured sensor package into it. Desktop then checks the package’s signature against the approved key for the selected vendor. If validation succeeds, Claude runs the vendor’s installation script, at most once per VM startup. Without the setting, nothing is installed. Approved vendors are CrowdStrike, Evoke Security, Neo, Palo Alto Networks, Pluto Security, SentinelOne, and Tanium. The installed sensor connects to its vendor’s cloud and reports activity. Its telemetry can leave the VM outside Cowork’s network allowlist, an important detail for teams reviewing outbound data flows. Administrators need Claude Desktop version 4.4212.0 or later. Windows deployments require the MSIX build, Windows 10 or 11, hardware virtualization, and Virtual Machine Platform enabled. Configuration uses mobile device management on macOS or registry policies on Windows, including Group Policy or Intune. Vendors provide their own packages and instructions. The sensor can access prompts, files, Claude responses, and other content inside the VM. That data goes to the EDR vendor, not Anthropic. Organizations therefore need to review vendor data handling alongside detection coverage. Anthropic also requires customers to test the software before deployment and after Claude or sensor updates. Removing management settings does not uninstall an existing sensor. It stops package execution at later VM starts. Package signatures expire within two years and do not cover updates downloaded afterward. Anthropic charges nothing extra during beta, although vendors may charge. For defenders, the benefit is clearer local visibility, not complete coverage of every Cowork session. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Breach WorkOS and Access Customer Slack Conversations
items.summary: WorkOS has confirmed unauthorized access to an internal sales application, exposing customer contact information and records of business conversations. The company detected the incident on October 30, 2026, and published a security bulletin on November 2. Its investigation identified an AI-assisted offensive security framework used to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts. Founder and CEO Michael Grinich said the attack involved ARTEX, an AI-powered framework that automates offensive security tasks. His statement on X adds detail to the company’s security bulletin, which describes an AI-assisted framework that automates reconnaissance and exploitation attempts without naming the tool. The affected application provided access to names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, and company affiliations stored in customer relationship management systems. It also contained customer account histories and sales relationship information. Customer communications included summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations. Operational metadata covered customers’ use of WorkOS products, including product usage and connection or directory health. WorkOS Confirms Data Breach These categories describe information available through the application, not a confirmed record-by-record account of everything accessed. WorkOS is reviewing affected records to determine the impact on individual organizations. The statement supplied with the disclosure says there is no evidence that WorkOS application data or production services were accessed or impacted. The investigation currently points to CRM and customer support information. The incident comes amid growing abuse of automated security-testing tools. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant describe ARTEX as a multi-agent platform that turns broad attacker goals into commands. Its agents can test permissions, map networks, adjust failed commands, and continue through several attack stages with limited human input. Earlier Cyber Security News coverage of ARTEX agents explains how attackers have used the framework for Active Directory discovery, credential attacks, and lateral movement. These are observations from separate investigations, not confirmed steps in the WorkOS breach. Wiz research also documented agents downloading application files, discovering internal API routes, and testing authentication controls. Related coverage of ARTEX targeting Microsoft 365 shows how stolen application credentials can support attacks across customer environments. Neither report establishes attribution for WorkOS. WorkOS disabled external access to the affected application, began reviewing access controls across internal tools, and retained an independent digital forensics and incident response firm. It will contact affected customers directly as findings are verified. Exposed conversation details could make phishing messages more convincing. WorkOS advises customers to verify unexpected requests before sharing sensitive information or taking action, even when messages reference real colleagues or support discussions. WorkOS has confirmed unauthorized access to an internal sales application, exposing customer contact information and records of business conversations. The company detected the incident on October 30, 2026, and published a security bulletin on November 2. Its investigation identified an AI-assisted offensive security framework used to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.

Founder and CEO Michael Grinich said the attack involved ARTEX, an AI-powered framework that automates offensive security tasks. His statement on X adds detail to the company’s security bulletin, which describes an AI-assisted framework that automates reconnaissance and exploitation attempts without naming the tool.

The affected application provided access to names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, and company affiliations stored in customer relationship management systems. It also contained customer account histories and sales relationship information.

Customer communications included summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations. Operational metadata covered customers’ use of WorkOS products, including product usage and connection or directory health.

WorkOS Confirms Data Breach

These categories describe information available through the application, not a confirmed record-by-record account of everything accessed.

WorkOS is reviewing affected records to determine the impact on individual organizations. The statement supplied with the disclosure says there is no evidence that WorkOS application data or production services were accessed or impacted. The investigation currently points to CRM and customer support information.

The incident comes amid growing abuse of automated security-testing tools. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant describe ARTEX as a multi-agent platform that turns broad attacker goals into commands. Its agents can test permissions, map networks, adjust failed commands, and continue through several attack stages with limited human input.

Earlier Cyber Security News coverage of ARTEX agents explains how attackers have used the framework for Active Directory discovery, credential attacks, and lateral movement. These are observations from separate investigations, not confirmed steps in the WorkOS breach.

Wiz research also documented agents downloading application files, discovering internal API routes, and testing authentication controls. Related coverage of ARTEX targeting Microsoft 365 shows how stolen application credentials can support attacks across customer environments. Neither report establishes attribution for WorkOS.

WorkOS disabled external access to the affected application, began reviewing access controls across internal tools, and retained an independent digital forensics and incident response firm. It will contact affected customers directly as findings are verified.

Exposed conversation details could make phishing messages more convincing. WorkOS advises customers to verify unexpected requests before sharing sensitive information or taking action, even when messages reference real colleagues or support discussions.

items.title: Google Dismantles 1.3 Million Device XCPE Botnet, Bans Android TV Maker Over Preinstalled Malware
items.summary: Google and industry partners have dismantled the XCPE botnet, which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes through preinstalled malware. In a November 2 report, Google linked the operation with high confidence to Videostrong Technology, accusing the Android device maker of deliberately building and running the backdoor for profit. According to Google’s technical investigation, Videostrong sold access to criminal affiliates that installed advertising fraud tools, proxy software, and further malware. Google banned the company, including future subsidiaries and affiliates, from producing certified Android devices or supplying software to certified vendors. 1.3 Million Device XCPE Botnet Dismantled The backdoor, named x.cpe or com.oemservice , was built into device firmware and ran with Android system privileges. Removing its installed package did not clear the infection because it could reinstall from the /oem/ partition after a reboot. Google said hidden code loaded after first boot helped bypass security checks. Its three-stage design separated remote control from malware execution. The backdoor passed instructions to com.abc.nexus , a loader that configured affiliate modules. XCPE Botnet Architecture (Source: Google) Those modules turned devices into proxy exit points, generated fake advertising views, or installed more backdoors. This separation also helped keep malicious activity harder to detect. Control traffic used MQTT, a lightweight messaging protocol. Google identified mqtt.szbboys[.]com on ports 3885–3887. Operators could silently install apps, execute shell commands, capture screens, and inspect networks. Researchers also observed stolen account details and system logs, injected keystrokes, and commands that opened remote shell access. The malware could disable Google Play Protect verification. Disruption Reaches Beyond XCPE Google worked with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI. Legal action targeted XCPE servers and control domains serving more than a dozen affiliate malware families. Google estimates these wider takedowns will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, separate from XCPE’s 1.3 million boxes. The findings follow earlier Google legal action against BadBox 2.0 , which affected over 10 million uncertified Android devices. Earlier BADBOX infections involving 190,000 Android devices also exposed the risks of compromised connected hardware. These earlier counts should not be combined with XCPE’s total. Most XCPE infections involved Android TV boxes, but researchers also found affected telehealth equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signs. Google has changed its device review process and is improving firmware integrity checks following the discovery. The takedown disrupts control infrastructure, rather than proving every device is clean. Google urges buyers to choose reputable manufacturers, consult its certified partner list , use trusted app stores, and keep Play Protect enabled. It also warns against apps offering payment for sharing unused bandwidth. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Quickpost: Banana Equivalent Dose
items.summary: From the Banana equivalent dose article in Wikipedia: The major natural source of radioactivity in plant tissue is potassium: 0.0117% of the naturally occurring potassium is the unstable isotope potassium-40. This isotope decays with a half-life of about 1.25 billion years (4×1016 seconds), and therefore the radioactivity of natural potassium is about 31 becquerel/gram (Bq/g), meaning that, in one gram of the element, about 31 atoms will decay every second. … Since a typical banana contains about half a gram of potassium, it will have an activity of roughly 15 Bq. Although the amount in a single banana is small in environmental and medical terms, the radioactivity from a truckload of bananas is capable of causing a false alarm when passed through a Radiation Portal Monitor used to detect possible smuggling of nuclear material at U.S. ports Of course, when I read this, I wanted to measure bananas with my meters. When looking at instant measurements (CPS and µSv/h), I noticed no increase. And the spectrum measured with my Radiacode 103 over 24 hours showed a minuscule little bump. It’s almost not noticeable in this spectrum, but when switching from log to linear, it stands out better: This bump is around 1460 keV, which corresponds to potassium 40: But it turns out that this bump is most likely not caused by potassium in the bananas, because it also shows up in a spectrum I measured of the background radiation, away from the bananas: Although this spectrum is measured at the same location as the banana measurement was done, it was measured 24 hours later, so there is no absolute guarantee that the background radiation was the same at that time. But I do know that my meter can pick up radiation from potassium 40. Here is a spectrum over 5 hours that I took with my meter stuck in low-sodium salt. In this salt, the sodium in sodium chloride has been replaced by potassium. Thus the concentration of potassium 40 is much higher than in bananas. Here you can see a little bump that doesn’t show up in the background radiation spectrum. Quickpost info
items.summary_html:
From the Banana equivalent dose article in Wikipedia:

The major natural source of radioactivity in plant tissue is potassium: 0.0117% of the naturally occurring potassium is the unstable isotope potassium-40. This isotope decays with a half-life of about 1.25 billion years (4×1016 seconds), and therefore the radioactivity of natural potassium is about 31 becquerel/gram (Bq/g), meaning that, in one gram of the element, about 31 atoms will decay every second. … Since a typical banana contains about half a gram of potassium, it will have an activity of roughly 15 Bq. Although the amount in a single banana is small in environmental and medical terms, the radioactivity from a truckload of bananas is capable of causing a false alarm when passed through a Radiation Portal Monitor used to detect possible smuggling of nuclear material at U.S. ports

Of course, when I read this, I wanted to measure bananas with my meters.

When looking at instant measurements (CPS and µSv/h), I noticed no increase.

And the spectrum measured with my Radiacode 103 over 24 hours showed a minuscule little bump.

It’s almost not noticeable in this spectrum, but when switching from log to linear, it stands out better:

This bump is around 1460 keV, which corresponds to potassium 40:

But it turns out that this bump is most likely not caused by potassium in the bananas, because it also shows up in a spectrum I measured of the background radiation, away from the bananas:

Although this spectrum is measured at the same location as the banana measurement was done, it was measured 24 hours later, so there is no absolute guarantee that the background radiation was the same at that time.

But I do know that my meter can pick up radiation from potassium 40. Here is a spectrum over 5 hours that I took with my meter stuck in low-sodium salt. In this salt, the sodium in sodium chloride has been replaced by potassium. Thus the concentration of potassium 40 is much higher than in bananas.

Here you can see a little bump that doesn’t show up in the background radiation spectrum.
